title: Punjabi Woman Navneet Kaur Shot Dead in Toronto, Brampton Man Charged With First-Degree Murder
excerpt: Family alleges the accused, a married man, had been harassing and pressuring the 26-year-old to marry him. She had returned to Punjab months earlier out of fear before going back to Canada.
body:
• Navneet Kaur, a 26-year-old woman from Punjab, was fatally shot in Toronto on July 24 in what police have classified as a targeted killing.
  • Sharandeep Singh, 37, a Brampton resident, has been arrested and charged with first-degree murder and breaching a court undertaking.
  • The victim's family alleges Singh — a married father — had been pressuring Kaur to marry him; she had returned to Punjab months earlier out of fear before coming back to Canada.
  • The case marks Toronto's 22nd homicide of 2026, adding to growing concerns about the safety of Indian nationals in Canada.

A 26-year-old woman from Punjab was shot dead on a Toronto street early Thursday morning in what police have described as a targeted killing, the latest in a series of violent incidents that have shaken the Indian diaspora in Canada.

Navneet Kaur was pronounced dead at the scene near Humberwood Boulevard and Rexdale Boulevard in Toronto's northwest end after a man spoke with her briefly and then opened fire at close range, according to Toronto Police. The shooting occurred around 7:23 a.m. on July 24.

Sharandeep Singh, 37, a resident of Brampton, Ontario, was arrested by the Ontario Provincial Police after fleeing the scene. He has been charged with first-degree murder and breaching a court undertaking — a detail that suggests the accused was already under judicial conditions at the time of the killing. Singh appeared before the Ontario Court of Justice on July 25.

Family Points to Harassment and Rejected Marriage Demands

Kaur's family has painted a disturbing picture of persistent harassment leading up to the shooting. According to her cousin, Malkeet Singh, the accused had known Navneet through their workplace in Canada. Despite being already married with children, Singh had repeatedly pressured her to marry him after divorcing his wife.

https://x.com/6ixbuzztv/status/2081054289179353339

"She had lodged a complaint with Canadian police about his harassment. We also contacted his family in India — even they admitted they were troubled by his conduct."

— Malkeet Singh, Navneet Kaur's cousin

When Kaur rejected his advances, the family alleges, Singh began harassing and threatening her. The escalating situation drove Kaur to return to Punjab roughly two to three months ago to distance herself from the accused. After spending time with her family, she returned to Canada to resume her career — a decision that proved fatal.

Questions Over Police Response

The family has raised pointed questions about the adequacy of the Canadian police response to Kaur's earlier complaints. They believe the killing could have been prevented had authorities acted more firmly on her reports of harassment and threats. The detail that Singh was charged with breaching a court undertaking raises further questions about whether existing judicial safeguards were sufficient to protect her.

Toronto Police have not publicly commented on Kaur's prior complaints or the nature of the court undertaking that Singh allegedly breached. Investigators said the initial probe confirms this was a targeted shooting, though they have not shared official details about the motive. The investigation is ongoing, and police have appealed to the public for CCTV and dashcam footage from the area.

A Growing Pattern of Violence

The killing marks Toronto's 22nd homicide of 2026 and adds to a deeply troubling pattern of violence against Indian nationals in Canada. In February, Chandan Kumar Raja Nandakumar, a 37-year-old IT professional from Karnataka, was killed in a targeted shooting in a Toronto parking lot. In late 2025, a 20-year-old doctoral student was gunned down near the University of Toronto Scarborough campus. Three Indian immigrants were killed in separate incidents across British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Alberta in early 2026.

According to data provided to India's Parliament, at least 17 Indian students died in violent attacks in Canada between 2018 and 2025. Gun murders across Canada have surged nearly 90 percent over the past decade, fueled in part by illegal firearms flowing across the U.S. border. Toronto Police data shows 88 percent of guns seized in crimes last year originated in the United States.

What Comes Next

Singh's next court appearance has not been publicly announced, but first-degree murder charges in Canada carry a mandatory life sentence with no eligibility for parole for 25 years upon conviction. The charge requires prosecutors to demonstrate that the killing was planned and deliberate — a threshold the details of this case may well meet.

For the Indian community in Canada, numbering over 1.3 million according to Statistics Canada, the case reinforces fears that existing protections for vulnerable individuals remain inadequate. Community leaders have repeatedly called for stronger intervention in domestic violence and harassment cases and swifter police action when complaints are filed.
nri_angle: The shooting of a 26-year-old Punjabi woman in Toronto adds to a troubling pattern of violence against Indian nationals in Canada, intensifying safety concerns across the diaspora.
